title: Nvidia is about 6% of the S&P 500. If Jensen Huang is ousted, there’s no clear successor — could chaos hit portfolios?
detail:
Nvidia is about 6% of the S&P 500. If Jensen Huang is ousted, there’s no clear successor — could chaos hit portfolios?
Mike Crisolago
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 5:00 PM CST 4 min read
NVDA
^GSPC
AAPL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia president and CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang already triggered a company investigation that could topple the world's most famous AI ambassador. But given the GPU giant also makes up more than 6% of the entire S&P 500, behind only Apple, investors are rightly wondering what the fallout means for their portfolios.

Nvidia stock dropped 6.39% on Monday morning following the Sunday letter Huang sent to employees apologizing for the affair (without mentioning the other party), and reaffirming his commitment to the company.

The company didn't respond to Moneywise's request for comment, but a spokesperson reiterated that the news "will not slow Nvidia," while the board said they have "no reason to believe" that Nvidia secrets or national security were compromised.

They also, however, have no succession plan for Huang, whose job hangs in the balance and whose ouster, Reuters warned, could lead to "a full blown leadership ⁠crisis."

Could Nvidia's leadership woes become a problem for your portfolio?

Escalating concerns over the pace of AI already caused Nvidia's stock to take a 22% hit last month. It remains the world's second-most valuable company, at $4.5 trillion, however, as its AI chips are central to the global data center buildout.

Yet given Fidelity's note that the 10 largest stocks, including Nvidia, "accounted for nearly 40% of the S&P 500 Index" in June, many investors may not realize how tied their portfolio is to the company's fortunes.

Investigations, of course, still need to be completed — which could include fresh scrutiny from the incoming Democrat-controlled Senate and Congress.

Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors

But Gary Black, managing partner with The Future Fund LLC, wrote on X that, while he doubts Huang will remain as Nvidia CEO and has no successor, he doesn't "see long-term value impairment." He acknowledged, though, that "many portfolio managers will reduce their Nvidia holdings in the coming weeks as a result of uncertainty" over the situation.

Why Nvidia's board is investigating Jensen Huang

On Sunday, Nvidia's board of directors said it was opening a probe into recent reports that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. What the Jensen Huang probe could mean for Nvidia stock

The story broke at an already sensitive time for chipmakers and the AI trade. Three House Republican committee chairs have already asked Jensen Huang for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and it's possible that more thorough investigations follow.

Image source: Getty Images.

Micron and chip stocks rebound after midterm sell-off

The Democratic win in last Tuesday's midterms raised worries about the AI data-center build-out. Many successful candidates ran on promises of increased scrutiny of data center permitting or outright moratoriums on new builds, including candidates in key states like Texas and Ohio.

The business looks as strong as it's ever been, but in my mind, last week's drop shows just how much of the stock price is based on perception. Grab Holdings (NASDAQ:GRAB), a Southeast Asian super-app for ride-hailing, delivery, and fintech services, closed at $3.44, up 0.88%. Investors were weighing Q3 revenue above estimates, record adjusted EBITDA, and fresh AI infrastructure plans.

Trading volume reached 88.9 million shares, coming in about 42% above its three-month average of 62.6 million shares. Grab Holdings IPO'd in 2020 and has fallen 71% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) closed at 7,550, up 2.35%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) closed at 25,253, up 2.74%. Among internet services and mobility/food delivery platforms, Uber Technologies (NYSE:UBER) closed at $71.17, up 3.76%, while Lyft (NASDAQ:LYFT) closed at $16.76, down 1.93%.

What this means for investors

Grab stock edged up on Monday, Nov. 9, after the company and SoftBank Group announced a joint agreement to develop artificial intelligence infrastructure in Malaysia, expanding Grab's role in Southeast Asia's AI buildout. The project seeks to construct one of the largest AI infrastructure facilities of its kind in the region.

This announcement added to investor optimism about the company's third-quarter earnings release on Nov. 3. Grab reported Q3 revenue of $1.1 billion, which represented 27% year-over-year growth, and record adjusted EBITDA of $237 million, a strong 73% year-over-year jump. Moreover, its adjusted free cash flow nearly doubled year over year to $533 million on a trailing twelve-month basis.

Last week's Q3 2026 results included raised full-year guidance. That helped drive the stock's latest rerating after the company beat expectations on earnings and outlook.

However, Grab suffered a setback last month when its attempt to acquire Taiwan-based Foodpanda from Delivery Hero was rejected by the Taiwanese government as anticompetitive. The country's food delivery market is dominated by Uber and Foodpanda. Uber has a stake in Grab, so blocking the acquisition makes sense. On the plus side, Grab gains a $60 million breakup fee and keeps $550 million in cash it would have used in the deal.
